title: Buffers, windows, tabs, many files
goal: Work across a whole project from one vim: switch files instantly, split the screen, and change many files in one command.

lessons.title: Buffers

concepts.desc: open (or create) a file in the current window.
list buffers: % is current, # is alternate, + is modified.
switch to buffer N, or by part of its name (Tab completes).
next / previous buffer.
toggle between the current and the alternate (previous) file.
write all / quit all / write and quit all buffers.
delete (close) the current buffer.

lessons.tip: A buffer is an open file; a window is just a view onto one. Neovim keeps modified buffers hidden when you switch, so :b away freely and :wa at the end.

quiz.q: Jump back and forth between the last two files you were in.
Switch to the buffer whose name contains 'router'.
In :ls output, what do % and # mean?
quiz.a: % is the current buffer, # the alternate buffer.

quiz.q: Save every modified buffer at once.
Go to the next buffer in the list.
What happens with `:e notes.md` if notes.md doesn't exist?
quiz.a: Vim opens an empty buffer for it; the file is created when you write it.

lessons.title: Windows and splits

concepts.desc: split horizontally / vertically (without a file: split the current one).
move to the window left / down / up / right (Ctrl-w h/j/k/l also works).
cycle through windows / go to the previous window.
close this window / close all others (only).
equalize sizes / maximize height / maximize width.
split the current window horizontally / vertically.

lessons.tip: Registers are shared across windows: yank in one split, paste in another. Closing a window never closes the buffer - it's still in :ls.

quiz.q: Open utils.js in a vertical split.
Move to the window on the right.
Close every window except the current one.
Make all windows the same size.
What does Ctrl-w c do to the buffer shown in that window?
quiz.a: Nothing - only the window closes; the buffer stays loaded.

quiz.q: Jump back to the window you were in before.

lessons.title: Tabs and the argument list

concepts.desc: open a file in a new tab page (a tab holds its own window layout).
next / previous tab / go to tab N.
close this tab / close all other tabs.
show / set the argument list (the files vim was started with).
run a command in every argument file and save the changed ones.
the same for every open buffer.

lessons.tip: Add the e flag in :argdo %s/a/b/ge so files without a match don't stop the run with an error.

quiz.q: Replace foo with bar in every argument file and save them.
Go to the next tab.
Why the `e` flag in `%s/foo/bar/ge` under :argdo?
quiz.a: So files with no match don't raise an error that aborts the run.

quiz.q: Make the argument list all Markdown files in the current directory.
What's the difference between :argdo and :bufdo?
quiz.a: :argdo runs over the argument list, :bufdo over every listed buffer.

quiz.q: Go straight to tab 3.

lessons.title: :vimgrep and the quickfix list

concepts.desc: search files recursively; matches go into the quickfix list and vim jumps to the first.
open / close the quickfix window (Enter on a line jumps there).
next / previous match.
first / last match.
run a command on every match line and save.
run it once per file in the list (e.g. :cfdo %s/a/b/g | update).

lessons.tip: vimgrep + cdo is project-wide search and replace with no plugins: :vimgrep /old/ **/*.js then :cdo s/old/new/ | update.

quiz.q: Search all .ts files under the current directory for 'TODO'.
Go to the next quickfix match.
Show the list of all matches.
Replace old with new on every match line and save.
Difference between :cdo and :cfdo?
quiz.a: :cdo runs per match (line), :cfdo once per file.

quiz.q: What does `**` mean in a vimgrep file pattern?

lessons.title: Week 9 review

concepts.desc: buffers
windows
tabs and argument list
project search and replace

lessons.tip: Use one buffer per file, windows when you need two side by side, and quickfix whenever the job is 'every place where X'.

quiz.q: Rename a function in every .go file under the current directory and save.
Open config.yaml next to the current file, side by side.
Return to the file you were editing just before this one.
Close the current window only.
Quit vim, saving all buffers.
List open buffers.
